function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “what‑to‑do” guide that you can copy‑paste into your local clone of the repository.  
I’ve written the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and a GitHub Actions workflow that will build the image whenever you push to `main`.  
After you add the files to the repo, just commit and push as usual.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repo (if you haven’t already)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Alpine is small and secure
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first so we can cache npm install
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on (adjust if needed)
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the official lightweight `node:18-alpine` image.  
> * Caches `npm ci` by copying only the `package*.json` files first.  
> * Exposes port `3000` – the default port used by the sample app.  
> * Starts the app with `node app.js`.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s.yaml` (or split into two files if you prefer) with the following content:

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80.  
> * Uses the image that will be pushed to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
>   Replace `${{ github.repository_owner }}` with your GitHub username if you’re not using the workflow variable.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# ------------------------------------
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (optional – remove if you don’t have tests)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Push Docker image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Installs Node.js 18, installs deps, runs tests, builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, logs into GHCR and pushes the image.  
> * The image will be available at `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:<sha>`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you prefer separate YAML files for deployment and service, adjust the `git add` command accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image and push it to GHCR.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Verify the Dockerfile**  
   ```bash
   docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .
   docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 test-nodejs-welcome
   ```
   Open `http://localhost:3000` – you should see the welcome page.

2. **Deploy to a cluster** (if you have one)  
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
   kubectl get pods
   kubectl get svc
   ```

---

That’s it!  
If you run into any issues (e.g., the app listens on a different port), just tweak the `EXPOSE` line in the Dockerfile and the `containerPort`/`targetPort` values in the Kubernetes YAML. Happy coding!
